title: Persian words in English
intro: You have been speaking Persian all your life without knowing it. Bazaar, caravan, paradise, pyjamas, checkmate, lemon, sugar, khaki – about forty everyday English words came from Persian or passed through it on their way west. This lesson follows them along the four great routes they travelled: through Greek and Latin, through Arabic and medieval Europe, through Ottoman Turkish, and through British India. Where etymologists disagree, we say so.
goals: give the Persian original of about forty English words and say what it meant
describe the four routes by which Persian words reached English
tell a well-established etymology from a probable or disputed one
talk about word origins in Persian: ریشه، وام‌واژه، از راه … به … رسید

sections.title: Words travel like caravans
sections.intro: An essay on how Persian words reached English. Watch the vocabulary of journeys – راه، مسیر، رسیدن، رساندن، بازگشتن – used for words, and the hedging (به نظر می‌رسد، اختلاف دارند) where the story is uncertain.

sentences.r: vāzhe-hā niz mānand-e kārvān-hā safar mi-konand.
sentences.en: Words, too, travel like caravans.

sentences.fa: بسیاری از واژه‌های انگلیسی که امروز کاملاً بومی به نظر می‌رسند، ریشه در زبان فارسی دارند.

sentences.en: Many English words that seem entirely native today have their roots in Persian.

sentences.fa: این واژه‌ها از چهار راه اصلی به انگلیسی رسیده‌اند.
sentences.r: in vāzhe-hā az chahār rāh-e asli be engelisi reside-and.
sentences.en: These words reached English by four main routes.

sentences.fa: راه نخست، یونانی و لاتین بود: یونانیان باستان واژه‌ی «پردیس» را از زبان‌های ایرانی باستان گرفتند و از آن «پارادایس» ساخته شد.

sentences.en: The first route was Greek and Latin: the ancient Greeks took the word pardis from the ancient Iranian languages, and from it came 'paradise'.

sentences.fa: این واژه در اصل به معنای باغی بود که گرداگردش دیوار کشیده بودند.
sentences.r: in vāzhe dar asl be ma'nā-ye bāgh-i bud ke gerdāgerd-ash divār keshide budand.

sentences.fa: «مغ»، نام روحانیان ایران باستان، نیز از همین راه به واژه‌ی «مجیک» در انگلیسی رسید.
sentences.r: «magh», nām-e ruhāniyān-e Irān-e bāstān, niz az hamin rāh be vāzhe-ye «mejik» dar engelisi resid.
sentences.en: Magh, the name of the priests of ancient Iran, also travelled this road to become 'magic' in English.

sentences.fa: راه دوم، عربی و اروپای قرون وسطی بود.
sentences.r: rāh-e dovvom, arabi va orupā-ye ghorun-e vostā bud.
sentences.en: The second route was Arabic and medieval Europe.

sentences.fa: «شکر»، «قند» و «اسفناج» از فارسی به عربی و از عربی به زبان‌های اروپایی رفتند.
sentences.r: «shekar», «ghand» o «esfenāj» az fārsi be arabi va az arabi be zabān-hā-ye orupāyi raftand.
sentences.en: Shekar (sugar), ghand (candy) and esfenāj (spinach) went from Persian into Arabic and from Arabic into the languages of Europe.

sentences.fa: بازی شطرنج نیز با واژه‌هایش، از جمله «شاه»، «رخ» و «شاه‌مات»، همین مسیر را پیمود.
sentences.r: bāzi-ye shatranj niz bā vāzhe-hā-yash, az jomle «shāh», «rokh» o «shāh-māt», hamin masir rā peymud.
sentences.en: The game of chess, with its words – shāh, rokh and shāh-māt among them – took the same road.

sentences.fa: راه سوم، ترکی عثمانی بود که «کوشک»، «شغال» و «دلبند» را به اروپا رساند.
sentences.r: rāh-e sevvom, torki-ye osmāni bud ke «kushk», «shoghāl» o «dolband» rā be orupā resānd.
sentences.en: The third route was Ottoman Turkish, which carried kushk (pavilion), shoghāl (jackal) and dolband (turban) to Europe.

sentences.fa: از «دلبند»، یعنی پارچه‌ای که دور سر می‌پیچیدند، هم «توربان» ساخته شد و هم نام گل «تولیپ».

sentences.en: From dolband, the cloth wound round the head, came both 'turban' and the name of the tulip.

sentences.fa: راه چهارم، هند بود؛ در آن‌جا فارسی قرن‌ها زبان دربار و دیوان بود.
sentences.r: rāh-e chahārom, Hend bud; dar ān-jā fārsi gharn-hā zabān-e darbār o divān bud.
sentences.en: The fourth route was India, where for centuries Persian was the language of the court and the administration.

sentences.fa: انگلیسی‌ها در هند واژه‌هایی چون «پاجامه»، «شال» و «خاکی» را از زبان‌های محلی آموختند.

sentences.en: In India the British learned words such as pājāme, shāl and khāki from the local languages.

sentences.fa: سربازان بریتانیایی در هند از نخستین کسانی بودند که لباس «خاکی»، یعنی همرنگ خاک، پوشیدند.

sentences.en: British soldiers in India were among the first to wear 'khaki' – earth-coloured – uniforms.

sentences.fa: گاهی معنای واژه در سفر تغییر کرده است.
sentences.r: gāh-i ma'nā-ye vāzhe dar safar taghyir karde ast.
sentences.en: Sometimes a word's meaning changed on the journey.

sentences.fa: «دیوان» در فارسی دفتر شعر یا اداره‌ی دولتی است، اما در انگلیسی به نوعی کاناپه گفته می‌شود.

sentences.en: In Persian a divān is a collection of poems or a government office, but in English the word is used for a kind of sofa.

sentences.fa: در مورد برخی واژه‌ها، مانند «اسکارلت»، ریشه‌شناسان هنوز با هم اختلاف دارند.

sentences.en: About some words, such as 'scarlet', etymologists still disagree.

sentences.fa: با این همه، هر بار که انگلیسی‌زبانی از «بازار» یا «شکر» سخن می‌گوید، تکه‌ای از فارسی را بر زبان می‌آورد.

sentences.en: Even so, every time an English speaker talks about a 'bazaar' or 'sugar', a little piece of Persian passes their lips.

The sweet orange is پرتقال – named after Portugal.

sections.title: Markets, clothes and the home
sections.md:
The first family of words is the vocabulary of trade and dress – carried by merchants along the Silk Road and by the British in India. Notice the Persian compounds that English swallowed whole: [[کاروان‌سرا|kārvānsarā|caravan + palace]], [[کمربند|kamarband|waist + band]], [[شیر و شکر|shir o shekar|milk and sugar]].

Talking about origins in Persian, you need only a handful of patterns: [[… از واژه‌ی فارسی … آمده است|… az vāzhe-ye fārsi-ye … āmade ast|… comes from the Persian word …]], [[از راه ترکی به انگلیسی رسید|az rāh-e torki be engelisi resid|it reached English by way of Turkish]], [[در اصل به معنای … بود|dar asl be ma'nā-ye … bud|it originally meant …]].

sections.title: Kings, games, priests and numbers
sections.md:
The second family came mostly through Greek and Latin in antiquity and through Arabic in the Middle Ages. Chess is the star: the game came to Iran from India, and when it travelled on to the Arabs and to Europe it took its Persian vocabulary with it. The cry [[شاه مات|shāh māt]] is usually read as *the king is helpless* – Persian مات means dumbfounded – though some scholars connect it with Arabic *māta*, 'he died'. From [[شاه|shāh]] English also has *check*, *chess* and even *exchequer* (the royal treasury, whose accounts were reckoned on a chequered cloth).

Two entries are names rather than words. *Algorithm* comes from the name of the 9th-century mathematician **al-Khwarizmi** ([[خوارزمی|Khārazmi]]), from Khwarazm in Central Asia, whose name in Latin was *Algoritmi*; *algebra* comes from the Arabic title of his book (*al-jabr*).

sections.title: Gardens, kitchens and colours
sections.md:
The third family is the sweetest. Iran's gardens and kitchens gave Europe fruits, flowers, sweets and the names of colours – often by way of Arabic Spain and Sicily, then Italian and French. Watch the sounds change on the road: Persian [[نارنگ|nārang]] / [[نارنج|nāranj]] became Arabic *nāranj*, Italian *arancia*, French *orange* – the *n* of *a norange* was swallowed by the article. The *peach* is a special case: the word is not Persian at all but Latin *persicum (malum)*, 'the Persian (apple)'.

The colour words show how cautious we must be. *Azure* certainly comes from [[لاجورد|lājvard]], the blue stone, via Arabic and Medieval Latin. *Scarlet* is **possibly** from a Persian name for a fine cloth (*saqerlāt*), but other scholars derive it from Latin, so dictionaries mark it as uncertain.

sections.title: Tom's list
sections.intro: Tom, the Australian student in Tehran, goes to Tajrish bazaar with Mahsa and discovers how much Persian he already knew. A short narrative in standard written Persian.

sections.title: The Persianate world
sections.md:
Why did Persian words reach English by so many roads? Because for most of the last thousand years Persian was not only the language of Iran. From the 10th century to the 19th it was the prestige language of a vast **Persianate world** – the language of poetry, letters and government from Anatolia and the Caucasus through Central Asia to Bengal.

The Ottoman court in Istanbul read Persian poetry and filled Ottoman Turkish with Persian words; that is how [[کوشک|kushk]] and [[دلبند|dolband]] reached Europe as *kiosk* and *tulip*. The Mughal emperors of India wrote and governed in Persian, and the East India Company kept Persian as its official language until 1837; that is why British officers came home talking about *pyjamas*, *khaki* and *cummerbunds*. Before all this, Arab scholars and merchants had absorbed Persian words for sugar, spinach and oranges and passed them on to Spain, Sicily and the rest of Europe.

The traffic now runs mostly the other way. Modern Persian is full of English and French: [[ماشین|māshin|car (from French machine)]], [[کامپیوتر|kāmpyuter]], [[پیژامه|pizhāme]] – which is *pyjamas* coming home after a journey of two hundred years. Iranians enjoy these round trips, and telling an Iranian friend that *bazaar* and *paradise* are Persian is a reliable way to start a long conversation.

sections.title: Tips
items: Use this list as a memory hook: if you know 'khaki', you know خاک (earth); if you know 'pyjamas', you know پا (leg) and جامه (garment).
Beware of false etymologies. English 'bad' and Persian بد look identical but are generally treated as a coincidence; 'cash', 'caravel' and 'assassin' are not Persian at all.
When an etymology is uncertain, say so in Persian: «به احتمال زیاد از … آمده است» (most probably comes from…), «ریشه‌شناسان در این باره اختلاف دارند» (etymologists disagree about this).
شکر is two words: shekar 'sugar' and shokr 'thanks'. Context and the vowel you hear decide – a good example of why Persian readers need context to read unvowelled script.
The orange family is a trap: نارنج is the bitter orange, پرتقال (from 'Portugal') the sweet orange, نارنگی the tangerine.
If you want more, look for the Persian words in other European languages: German Basar, French paradis and échecs, Spanish naranja and azul – all from the same roots.
